metadata.title: A Local converse theorem for Archimedean $\GL(n)$

extraction_notes.note: The proofs of the two main theorems are written in prose across Sections 4 and 5 and their 'Step' subsections; following 'a proof continued elsewhere is one node per part', each subsection is its own proof node with a proves edge to the theorem and a uses edge to the section's opening part.

Section 2 recalls standard facts about Weil-group parameters and their local factors (reference: Tate); these computations are typed as claims with origin external rather than theorems, since the paper presents them as routine recalled facts.
The consistency check for phi_{0,t} appears twice verbatim (end of Section 2.4 and in Section 2.6); only the second copy, which ends a complete sentence and feeds (2.15), is a node.

Nien's finite-field analogue and Henniart's L/epsilon-factor characterization are only mentioned, not stated, and are not nodes; the intro and Section 6 restatements of Proposition 6.2 and of the sharpness claims get no separate nodes.
Equations (5.12)-(5.13) contain the index typo u_i on the right-hand side (should be u'_j); copied verbatim.

nodes.name: Henniart's local converse theorem
nodes.statement: If $F$ is non-archimedean, the first major result is the one by Henniart (\cite{Henniart1}) in which he shows that if two {\it generic} representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that \[ \gamma(s, \pi\otimes\tau, \psi)=\gamma(s, \pi'\otimes\tau, \psi) \] for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ for all $t=1,\dots,n-1$, where the $\gamma$-factor is the one defined by Jacquet, Piatetski-Shapiro and Shalika, then $\pi=\pi'$.
nodes.statement_short: For non-archimedean $F$, generic $\pi,\pi'$ with equal $\gamma$-factors under all $\operatorname{GL}_t$-twists, $t\le n-1$, are equal.
assumptions: two {\it generic} representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that \[ \gamma(s, \pi\otimes\tau, \psi)=\gamma(s, \pi'\otimes\tau, \psi) \] for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ for all $t=1,\dots,n-1$

nodes.name: Chen's n x (n-2) local converse theorem
nodes.statement: Later, in \cite{Chen} Chen improved this result by requiring $t$ be only up to $n-2$ with the extra assumption that $\pi$ and $\pi'$ have the same central character (we note that it was later known that $\operatorname{GL}_1$ twisting determines the central character; see, for example, \cite{JNS}).
nodes.statement_short: Twists up to $\operatorname{GL}_{n-2}$ suffice in Henniart's theorem when the central characters agree.
assumptions: the extra assumption that $\pi$ and $\pi'$ have the same central character

nodes.name: Jacquet's conjecture on the local converse problem
nodes.statement: It had been conjectured by Jacquet for some time that one only needs $t\leq[\frac{n}{2}]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Jacquet's conjecture (Chai; Jacquet-Liu)
nodes.statement: And very recently this conjecture has been proven by Chai in \cite{Chai}, and Jacquet and Liu in \cite{JL} (see also \cite{ALSX, JNS}).

nodes.name: Archimedean local converse theorem (complex case)
nodes.statement: Let $F=\mathbb C$. If the two representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ satisfy \[ L(s, \pi\times\chi)=L(s, \pi'\times\chi) \] for all characters $\chi$ on $\mathbb C^\times$, where the $L$-factors are of Artin type defined by the local Langlands correspondence, then $\pi=\pi'$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$, equality of Artin-type $L$-factors under all $\operatorname{GL}(1)$-twists forces $\pi=\pi'$.
assumptions: the two representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ satisfy \[ L(s, \pi\times\chi)=L(s, \pi'\times\chi) \] for all characters $\chi$ on $\mathbb C^\times$

nodes.name: Archimedean local converse theorem (real case)
nodes.statement: Let $F=\mathbb{R}$. If the two representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ satisfy \[ L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s, \pi'\times\tau) \] for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ with $t=1, 2$, where the $L$-factors are of Artin type defined by the local Langlands correspondence, then $\pi=\pi'$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb R)$, equality of Artin-type $L$-factors under all $\operatorname{GL}(1)$- and $\operatorname{GL}(2)$-twists forces $\pi=\pi'$.
assumptions: the two representations $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ satisfy \[ L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s, \pi'\times\tau) \] for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ with $t=1, 2$

nodes.name: Sharpness of GL(2)-twists for n=2
nodes.statement: We will show that for $F=\mathbb{R}$ the bound $t\leq 2$ is sharp even if $n=2$, namely one always needs $\operatorname{GL}(2)$-twists.
conclusions: the bound $t\leq 2$ is sharp even if $n=2$

nodes.name: GL(2)-twists needed for n>=4 even with central character
nodes.statement: However, even with the central character assumption, for $n\geq 4$ one always needs $\operatorname{GL}(2)$-twists, and indeed we will give an infinite family of nonequivalent representations of $\operatorname{GL}_4(\mathbb{R})$ which cannot be distinguished by $\operatorname{GL}(1)$-twists.
assumptions: even with the central character assumption

nodes.name: Genericity is necessary for gamma-factor converse theorems
nodes.statement: Let us note that the local converse theorems via gamma factors as in \cite{Henniart1, Chen, Chai, JL} all assume that the representations are generic. This is because gamma factors cannot distinguish the representations appearing in a same parabolically induced representation. Namely, all the constituents of a parabolically induced representation have the same gamma factor, and accordingly the genericity assumption is necessary.
nodes.statement_short: All constituents of a parabolically induced representation share a $\gamma$-factor, so $\gamma$-factor converse theorems need genericity.

nodes.name: Archimedean local converse theorem via gamma factors
nodes.statement: Of course, it makes sense to ask if it is possible to establish a local converse theorem for the archimedean case in terms of gamma factors, for generic representations. We will take up this issue in our later work.

nodes.name: F is R or C
nodes.statement: Throughout, $F$ is either $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb C$.

nodes.name: Irr_n
nodes.statement: We let $\operatorname{Irr}_n$ be the set of infinitesimal equivalence classes of irreducible admissible representations of $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$.

nodes.name: absolute value |z|
nodes.statement: For $z\in F$, we let $|z|=\sqrt{z\bar{z}}$, so that if $F=\mathbb{R}$, this is the absolute value of $z$, and if $F=\mathbb C$, it is the usual modulus of $z$.

nodes.name: norm ||z||
nodes.statement: We also let $\|z\|=z\bar{z}=|z|^2$.

nodes.name: character (quasi-character); Irr_1
nodes.statement: By a character, we always mean a quasi-character, and $\operatorname{Irr}_1$ is the set of characters of $F^\times$.

nodes.name: standard additive character psi_F
nodes.statement: We let $\psi_F$ be the standard choice of additive character on $F$; namely if $F=\mathbb{R}$, then $\psi_\mathbb{R}(r)=e^{2\pi i r}$, and if $F=\mathbb C$, then $\psi_\mathbb C(z)=\psi_\mathbb{R}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb C/\mathbb{R}}(z)=e^{2\pi i(z+\bar{z})}$.

nodes.name: gamma function
nodes.statement: We let $\Gamma(s)$ be the gamma function.

nodes.name: duplication formula
nodes.statement: Recall that $\Gamma(s)$ satisfies \[ \Gamma\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{s+1}{2}\right) =2^{1-s}\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(s),\quad\text{(duplication formula)}. \]

nodes.name: Poles and zeros of the gamma function
nodes.statement: Also recall that $\Gamma(s)$ has no zeroes, and has infinitely many poles, which are precisely at $s=0, -1, -2, \dots$ and all of which are simple.
conclusions: has infinitely many poles, which are precisely at $s=0, -1, -2, \dots$ and all of which are simple

nodes.name: Weil group W_F
nodes.statement: We let $W_F$ be the Weil group of $F$. So $W_\mathbb C=\mathbb C^\times$ and $W_\mathbb{R}=\mathbb C^\times\cup j\mathbb C^\times$ with $j^2=-1$ and $jzj^{-1}=\bar{z}$.

nodes.name: Abelianization of the Weil group
nodes.statement: Note that $F^\times\cong W_F^{ab}$.

nodes.name: Proof of F^x = W_F^ab
nodes.statement: This is obvious if $F=\mathbb C$. If $F=\mathbb{R}$, we have a surjective map \begin{equation} W_\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^\times, \quad z\mapsto z\bar{z},\; j\mapsto -1, \end{equation} whose kernel is the commutator group $[W_\mathbb{R}, W_\mathbb{R}]$, which is actually of the form $\{z\in\mathbb C^\times:|z|=1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial for $\mathbb C$; for $\mathbb R$ exhibit the surjection $W_\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^\times$ with kernel the commutator subgroup.

nodes.name: map W_R -> R^x
nodes.statement: W_\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^\times, \quad z\mapsto z\bar{z},\; j\mapsto -1,
nodes.label: E:W_R

nodes.name: characters chi_{-N,t} of C^x
nodes.statement: If $F=\mathbb C$, each character is of the form \[ \chi_{-N, t}(z):=z^{-N}\|z\|^t, \] where $N\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $t\in\mathbb C$.

nodes.name: Complex conjugate of chi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: Let us note that \[ \overline{\chi_{-N,t}}=\chi_{N, t-N}, \] where $\overline{\chi_{-N,t}}(z):=\overline{\chi_{-N,t}(z)}=\chi_{-N,t}(\bar{z})$ as usual.

nodes.name: characters lambda_{eps,t} of R^x
nodes.statement: If $F=\mathbb{R}$, each character is of the form \[ \lambda_{\varepsilon, t}(r):=r^{-\varepsilon}|r|^t=\operatorname{sign}(r)^{\varepsilon}|r|^{t-\varepsilon},\quad r\in\mathbb{R}^\times, \] where $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$, $t\in\mathbb C$ and $\operatorname{sign}$ is the sign character.

nodes.name: Representations of W_C
nodes.statement: If $F=\mathbb C$, an irreducible representation of $W_\mathbb C=\mathbb C^\times$ is 1-dimensional, namely a character on $\mathbb C^\times$, and hence of the form $\chi_{-N,t}$ as above. Then in general, an $n$-dimensional representation $\varphi:W_\mathbb C\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is of the form \begin{equation} \varphi=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}. \end{equation}
conclusions: an irreducible representation of $W_\mathbb C=\mathbb C^\times$ is 1-dimensional

nodes.name: general parameter over C
nodes.statement: \varphi=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}.
nodes.label: E:general_parameter_C

nodes.name: Irreducible representations of W_R have dimension 1 or 2
nodes.statement: If $F=\mathbb{R}$, an irreducible representation of $W_\mathbb{R}$ is 1 or 2 dimensional. If it is 1-dimensional, it factors through $W_\mathbb{R}^{ab}\cong\mathbb{R}^\times$ and hence is identified with a character of the form $\lambda_{\varepsilon, t}$.
conclusions: an irreducible representation of $W_\mathbb{R}$ is 1 or 2 dimensional

nodes.name: 2-dimensional parameters phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: If it is 2-dimensional, it is of the form \[ \varphi_{-N,t}:=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-N,t}. \]

nodes.name: Computation of det(phi_{-N,t})
nodes.statement: From the definition of $W_\mathbb{R}$, we can see that $\det(\varphi_{-N,t})(z)=\chi_{-N, t}(z\bar{z})=\|z\|^{-N+2t}$ for $z\in\mathbb C^\times\subseteq W_\mathbb{R}$, and $\det(\varphi_{-N,t})(j)=-\chi_{-N,t}(-1)=-(-1)^N$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct evaluation of the determinant on $z$ and on $j$.

nodes.name: Determinant of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: Hence from \eqref{E:W_R}, as a character on $\mathbb{R}^\times$ we can identify $\det(\varphi_{-N,t})$ with $\operatorname{sign}\chi_{-N, t}$ where $\chi_{-N, t}$ is viewed as a character on $\mathbb{R}^\times$ via the inclusion $\mathbb{R}^\times\subseteq\mathbb C^\times$. Namely \begin{equation} r\mapsto\operatorname{sign}(r) r^{-N}|r|^{2t}. \end{equation}
conclusions: as a character on $\mathbb{R}^\times$ we can identify $\det(\varphi_{-N,t})$ with $\operatorname{sign}\chi_{-N, t}$

nodes.name: determinant character of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: r\mapsto\operatorname{sign}(r) r^{-N}|r|^{2t}.
nodes.label: E:central_character

nodes.name: Decomposition of phi_{0,t}
nodes.statement: Let us mention that if $N=0$, the representation $\varphi_{-N,t}$ is not irreducible but we have \[ \varphi_{0, t}=\lambda_{0, t}\oplus\lambda_{1, t+1}. \]

nodes.name: phi_{-N,t} = phi_{N,t-N}
nodes.statement: Also since $\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-N,t}=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\overline{\chi_{-N,t}}$, we have \begin{equation} \varphi_{-N,t}=\varphi_{N, t-N}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: phi_{-N,t}=phi_{N,t-N}
nodes.statement: \varphi_{-N,t}=\varphi_{N, t-N}.
nodes.label: E:N>0

nodes.name: Irreducible 2-dimensional representations of W_R
nodes.statement: Hence we may assume $N>0$. Namely the irreducible 2-dimensional representations of $W_\mathbb{R}$ are precisely the representations of the form $\varphi_{-N,t}$ with $N>0$.
conclusions: the irreducible 2-dimensional representations of $W_\mathbb{R}$ are precisely the representations of the form $\varphi_{-N,t}$ with $N>0$

nodes.name: General n-dimensional representation of W_R
nodes.statement: In general, an $n$-dimensional representation $\varphi:W_\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is of the form \begin{equation} \varphi=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\right) \end{equation} where $N_i>0$ for all $i$, and $p+2q=n$.

nodes.name: general parameter over R
nodes.statement: \varphi=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\right)
nodes.label: E:general_parameter_R

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors of chi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb C$. Then the $L$- and $\epsilon$-factors of the character $\chi_{-N,t}$ are defined as \begin{align} \notag L(\chi_{-N, t})&=2(2\pi)^{-(t-\frac{N}{2}+\frac{|N|}{2})}\Gamma(t-\frac{N}{2}+\frac{|N|}{2})\\ &=\begin{cases}2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t-N)}\Gamma(t-N),\quad\text{if $N<0$}, \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_\mathbb C)&=i^{|N|}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $L(\chi_{-N,t})$ is $2(2\pi)^{-u}\Gamma(u)$ with $u=t-N/2+|N|/2$, and $\epsilon=i^{|N|}$.

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors over C
nodes.statement: \notag L(\chi_{-N, t})&=2(2\pi)^{-(t-\frac{N}{2}+\frac{|N|}{2})}\Gamma(t-\frac{N}{2}+\frac{|N|}{2})\\ &=\begin{cases}2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t-N)}\Gamma(t-N),\quad\text{if $N<0$}, \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_\mathbb C)&=i^{|N|}.
nodes.label: E:L-factor-C

nodes.name: Local factors invariant under conjugation
nodes.statement: Let us note that \begin{equation*} L(\chi_{-N, t})=L(\overline{\chi_{-N, t}})\quad\text{and}\quad \epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_\mathbb C)=\epsilon(\overline{\chi_{-N,t}},\psi_\mathbb C). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Local factors of n-dimensional parameters of W_C
nodes.statement: In general, if $\varphi:W_\mathbb C\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is an $n$-dimensional representation as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_C}, we define the local factors multiplicatively as \begin{align*} L(\varphi)&=L(\chi_{-N_1,t_1})\cdots L(\chi_{-N_n, t_n}),\\ \epsilon(\varphi,\psi_\mathbb C) &=\epsilon(\chi_{-N_1,t_1}, \psi_\mathbb C)\cdots\epsilon(\chi_{-N_n, t_n}, \psi_\mathbb C). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Local factors of lambda_{eps,t}
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb{R}$. For the 1-dimensional $\lambda_{\varepsilon, t}$, \begin{align} L(\lambda_{\varepsilon,t})&=\pi^{-\frac{t}{2}}\Gamma\left(\frac{t}{2}\right),\\ \epsilon(\lambda_{\varepsilon,t},\psi_\mathbb{R})&=(-i)^\varepsilon. \end{align}

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors of lambda
nodes.statement: L(\lambda_{\varepsilon,t})&=\pi^{-\frac{t}{2}}\Gamma\left(\frac{t}{2}\right),\\ \epsilon(\lambda_{\varepsilon,t},\psi_\mathbb{R})&=(-i)^\varepsilon.
nodes.label: E:L-factor-R1

nodes.name: Local factors of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: For the 2-dimensional representation $\varphi_{-N,t}$, \begin{align} L(\varphi_{-N,t})&=L(\chi_{-N,t}) =\begin{cases}2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t-N)}\Gamma(t-N),\quad\text{if $N<0$}, \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N,t},\psi_\mathbb{R})&=-i\cdot\epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_\mathbb C)=-i^{|N|+1}. \end{align}

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: L(\varphi_{-N,t})&=L(\chi_{-N,t}) =\begin{cases}2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t-N)}\Gamma(t-N),\quad\text{if $N<0$}, \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N,t},\psi_\mathbb{R})&=-i\cdot\epsilon(\chi_{-N,t},\psi_\mathbb C)=-i^{|N|+1}.
nodes.label: E:L-factor-R2

nodes.name: Local factors of n-dimensional parameters of W_R
nodes.statement: In general, if $\varphi:W_\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is an $n$-dimensional representation as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_R}, we again define the local factors multiplicatively as \begin{align*} L(\varphi)&=L(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1})\cdots L(\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p})\cdot L(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1})\cdots L(\chi_{-N_q, u_q})\\ \epsilon(\varphi,\psi_\mathbb{R}) &=\epsilon(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}, \psi_\mathbb{R})\cdots\epsilon(\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}, \psi_\mathbb{R})\cdot \epsilon(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}, \psi_\mathbb{R})\cdots \epsilon(\chi_{-N_q, u_q},\psi_\mathbb{R}). \end{align*}

nodes.name: GL(1)-twist over C
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb C$. Let $\chi_{-M,s}$ be a character on $\mathbb C^\times$, and let $\varphi$ be an $n$-dimensional representation of $W_\mathbb C$ as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_C}. Then the twist $\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s}$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ is given by \begin{equation} \varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s} =\chi_{-(N_1+M), t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N_n+M), t_n+s}. \end{equation}
assumptions: Let $\chi_{-M,s}$ be a character on $\mathbb C^\times$
conclusions: the twist $\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s}$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ is given by

nodes.name: twisted parameter over C
nodes.statement: \varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s} =\chi_{-(N_1+M), t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N_n+M), t_n+s}.
nodes.label: E:twisted_general_parameter_C

nodes.name: GL(1)-twist of lambda_{eps,t}
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb{R}$. Let $\lambda_{\delta, s}$ be a character on $\mathbb{R}^\times$. For the 1-dimensional parameter $\lambda_{\varepsilon,t}$, the twist by $\lambda_{\delta,s}$ is given by \[ \lambda_{\varepsilon, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}= \lambda_{\varepsilon+\delta\,(\operatorname{mod} 2),\, t+s-\gamma}, \;\text{ where }\; \gamma=\begin{cases}2\quad\text{if $\varepsilon=\delta=1$};\\ 0,\quad\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

nodes.name: GL(1)-twist of phi_{-N,t}
nodes.statement: For the 2-dimensional parameter $\varphi_{-N,t}=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-N, t}$, the twisted parameter $\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}$ is computed as \begin{align*} \varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s} &=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}(\chi_{-N, t}\otimes(\lambda_{\delta, s}\circ N_{\mathbb C/\mathbb{R}}))\\ &=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}(\chi_{-N, t}\otimes\chi_{0, s-\delta})\\ &=\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-N, t+s-\delta}, \end{align*} namely \[ \varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}=\varphi_{-N, t+s-\delta}. \]

nodes.name: Local factors of GL(2)xGL(1)
nodes.statement: Accordingly, we have \begin{align} L(\varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s})&=\begin{cases} 2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta-N)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta-N) \quad\text{if $N<0$}; \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}, \psi_\mathbb{R})&=-i^{|N|+1}. \end{align}

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors of phi twisted by lambda
nodes.statement: L(\varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s})&=\begin{cases} 2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta),\quad\text{if $N\geq 0$};\\ 2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta-N)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta-N) \quad\text{if $N<0$}; \end{cases}\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N, t}\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}, \psi_\mathbb{R})&=-i^{|N|+1}.
nodes.label: E:GL(2)xGL(1)_L

nodes.name: GL(1)-twist of a general parameter over R
nodes.statement: If $\varphi:W_\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is an $n$-dimensional representation as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_R}, we have \[ \varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}= \left(\lambda_{\delta_1,t_1+s-\gamma_1} \oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\delta_p,t_p+s-\gamma_p}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1+s-\delta}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q+s-\delta}\right), \] where $\delta_i=\varepsilon_i+\delta\pmod{2}$, and $\gamma_i=2$ if $\varepsilon_i=\delta=1$ and $\gamma_i=0$ otherwise.
assumptions: $\varphi:W_\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ is an $n$-dimensional representation as in \eqref{E:general_parameter_R}

nodes.name: Tensor product of two 2-dimensional parameters
nodes.statement: Assume $F=\mathbb{R}$. Let $\varphi_{-N,t}$ and $\varphi_{-M,s}$ be 2-dimensional representations of $W_\mathbb{R}$ as above with $N, M > 0$. Then one can see \begin{align*} \varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s}=& \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-N,t}\right)\otimes \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-M,s}\right)\\ =&\left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-N,t}\cdot\chi_{-M,s}\right)\oplus \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-N,t}\cdot\overline{\chi_{-M,s}}\right)\\ =&\left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-(N+M),t+s}\right)\oplus \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-N,t}\cdot\chi_{M,s-M}\right)\\ =&\varphi_{-(N+M), t+s}\oplus \left(\operatorname{Ind}_{W_\mathbb C}^{W_\mathbb{R}}\chi_{-(N-M),t+s-M}\right)\\ =&\varphi_{-(N+M), t+s}\oplus\varphi_{-(N-M), t+s-M}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Consistency of local factors of phi_{0,t}
nodes.statement: However, let us note that for the parameter $\varphi_{0, t}$, we can check that $L(\varphi_{0, t})=L(\chi_{0, t})=2(2\pi)^{-t}\Gamma(t)$, since it is indeed equal to $L(\lambda_{0,t})L(\lambda_{1,t+1})=\pi^{-t/2}\Gamma(\frac{t}{2})\cdot\pi^{-(t+1)/2}\Gamma(\frac{t+1}{2})$ by the duplication formula. Also one can check that $\epsilon(\varphi_{0,t})=-i\cdot\epsilon(\chi_{0,t},\psi_\mathbb C)=-i$, which is indeed equal to $\epsilon(\lambda_{0,t},\psi_\mathbb{R})\epsilon(\lambda_{1,t+1},\psi_\mathbb{R})=-i$.

nodes.name: Local factors of GL(2)xGL(2)
nodes.statement: Then, coupled together with the identity \[ \varphi_{-(N-M), t+s-M}=\varphi_{-(M-N), t+s-N} \] (by \eqref{E:N>0}), we obtain \begin{align} L(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})&=4(2\pi)^{-2(t+s)+\min\{N, M\}}\cdot\Gamma(t+s)\cdot \Gamma(t+s-\min\{N, M\})\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})&=(-1)^{\max\{N, M\}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $L(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})=4(2\pi)^{\cdots}\Gamma(t+s)\Gamma(t+s-\min\{N,M\})$ and $\epsilon=(-1)^{\max\{N,M\}}$.

nodes.name: L- and epsilon-factors of GL(2)xGL(2)
nodes.statement: L(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})&=4(2\pi)^{-2(t+s)+\min\{N, M\}}\cdot\Gamma(t+s)\cdot \Gamma(t+s-\min\{N, M\})\\ \epsilon(\varphi_{-N,t}\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})&=(-1)^{\max\{N, M\}}.
nodes.label: E:GL(2)xGL(2)_L

nodes.name: Archimedean local Langlands correspondence
nodes.statement: By the archimedean local Langlands correspondence, originally established by Langlands (\cite{Langlands}), there is a one-to-one correspondence between the set $\operatorname{Irr}_n$ and the set $\Phi_n$ of all continuous $n$-dimensional representations of $W_F$.
conclusions: there is a one-to-one correspondence between the set $\operatorname{Irr}_n$ and the set $\Phi_n$ of all continuous $n$-dimensional representations of $W_F$

nodes.name: Local factors of pairs (Artin type)
nodes.statement: If $\pi_1\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ and $\pi_2\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ correspond to $\varphi_1\in\Phi_n$ and $\varphi_2\in\Phi_t$, respectively, then the local factors are defined to be \begin{align*} L(s,\pi_1\times\pi_2)&=L(\varphi_1\otimes\varphi_2|\cdot|_F^s)\\ \epsilon(s,\pi_1\times\pi_2,\psi_F)&= \epsilon(\varphi_1\otimes\varphi_2|\cdot|_F^s,\psi_F), \end{align*} where $|\cdot|_{\mathbb C}=\|\cdot\|$ and $|\cdot|_{\mathbb{R}}=|\cdot|$.
nodes.statement_short: $L(s,\pi_1\times\pi_2)$ and $\epsilon$ are defined via the Langlands parameters as the factors of $\varphi_1\otimes\varphi_2|\cdot|_F^s$.

nodes.name: Central character equals determinant of the parameter
nodes.statement: Further if $\varphi\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ corresponds to $\varphi_\pi\in\Phi_n$ and if $\omega_\pi$ is the central character of $\pi$, we have \[ \omega_\pi=\det(\varphi_\pi). \]

nodes.name: Central character of GL_2(R) representation
nodes.statement: In particular, if $\pi$ is a representation of $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\varphi_\pi=\varphi_{-N,t}$, then $\omega_\pi$ is as in \eqref{E:central_character}.
assumptions: $\pi$ is a representation of $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\varphi_\pi=\varphi_{-N,t}$

nodes.name: partial order on C
nodes.statement: We define a partial order $\preceq$ on the set $\mathbb C$ of complex numbers as follows: For $t_1,t_2\in\mathbb C$, \[ t_1\preceq t_2\quad\text{if}\quad t_2-t_1\in\mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}, \] and otherwise we say they are \emph{incomparable}.

nodes.name: strict order
nodes.statement: We use the symbol $\prec$ for strict inequality, namely \[ t_1\prec t_2\quad\text{if}\quad t_1\preceq t_2\text{ but } t_1\neq t_2. \]

nodes.name: Order versus poles of gamma functions
nodes.statement: Then one can check that $t_1\prec t_2$ if and only if \begin{equation*} \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$}\}\supsetneq \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$}\}, \end{equation*} and $t_1$ and $t_2$ are incomparable if and only if \begin{equation*} \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$}\}\cap \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$}\}=\emptyset. \end{equation*}
conclusions: $t_1\prec t_2$ if and only if \begin{equation*} \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$}\}\supsetneq \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$}\}, \end{equation*}
$t_1$ and $t_2$ are incomparable if and only if \begin{equation*} \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$}\}\cap \{\text{poles of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$}\}=\emptyset. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: $t_1\prec t_2$ iff the poles of $\Gamma(s+t_1)$ strictly contain those of $\Gamma(s+t_2)$; incomparable iff the pole sets are disjoint.

nodes.name: minimal element
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a finite set of complex numbers and $t\in A$ is a minimal element in $A$ (\text{i.e.\ } whenever $t'\in A$ is such that $t'\preceq t$, we have $t'=t$), we say $t$ is {\it minimal in} $A$.
differentia: whenever $t'\in A$ is such that $t'\preceq t$, we have $t'=t$

nodes.name: maximal pole
nodes.statement: Let $F(s)$ be a function on $\mathbb C$. If $F(s)$ has a pole at $s=t$ and if it is maximal among the poles of $F(s)$ with respect to $\preceq$ (\text{i.e.\ } if $F(s)$ has a pole at $s=t'$ and $t\preceq t'$, then $t=t'$), then we call the pole at $s=t$ a {\it maximal pole} of $F(s)$.
differentia: it is maximal among the poles of $F(s)$ with respect to $\preceq$

nodes.name: Maximal pole of Gamma(s+t)
nodes.statement: In particular, for a fixed $t\in\mathbb C$, the gamma function $\Gamma(s+t)$ has a unique maximal pole at $s=-t$.
conclusions: the gamma function $\Gamma(s+t)$ has a unique maximal pole at $s=-t$

nodes.name: Maximal poles of a product of gamma functions
nodes.statement: More generally, a product $\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)$ of gamma functions has a maximal pole precisely at $s=-t_i$ where $t_i$ is a minimal element in the set $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$.
conclusions: a product $\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)$ of gamma functions has a maximal pole precisely at $s=-t_i$ where $t_i$ is a minimal element in the set $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$

nodes.name: Gamma product cancellation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $t_1,\dots, t_m, t'_1,\dots, t'_{m'}\in\mathbb C$. Suppose \begin{equation} F(s)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^m\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^{m'}\Gamma(s+t'_j) \end{equation} as functions in $s$, where $F(s)$ is a function on $\mathbb C$ whose zeros and poles do not interfere with the poles of the $\Gamma(s+t_i)$'s and $\Gamma(s+t'_i)$'s. Then $m=m'$, and further for each $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$, there is a corresponding $j\in\{1,\dots,m'\}$ such that $t_i=t'_j$, namely \[ \{t_1,\dots,t_m\}=\{t'_1,\dots,t'_{m'}\} \] as multisets. Accordingly, $F\equiv 1$.
nodes.statement_short: If $F(s)\prod\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod\Gamma(s+t'_j)$ with $F$ not interfering with poles, then the multisets $\{t_i\}$, $\{t'_j\}$ agree and $F\equiv1$.
assumptions: $F(s)$ is a function on $\mathbb C$ whose zeros and poles do not interfere with the poles of the $\Gamma(s+t_i)$'s and $\Gamma(s+t'_i)$'s
nodes.label: L:Lemma

nodes.name: gamma product identity
nodes.statement: F(s)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^m\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^{m'}\Gamma(s+t'_j)
nodes.label: E:Lemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: This is almost immediate if one looks at the maximal poles of both sides. Namely, if $t_k$ is minimal in $\{t_1,\cdots,t_m\}$, the left hand side has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$, and hence the right hand side has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$. But each maximal pole of the right hand side occurs at $s=-t'_l$ for some $t'_l$ which is minimal in $\{t'_1,\dots,t'_{m'}\}$. Hence $t_k=t'_l$ for some $l$. After reordering the indices, if necessary, we may assume $t_1=t'_1$. Hence \eqref{E:Lemma} is written as \[ F(s)\cdot\prod_{i=2}^m\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=2}^{m'}\Gamma(s+t'_j). \] By arguing inductively, one proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the number of factors: match a maximal pole on both sides, cancel the corresponding gamma factors, repeat.

nodes.name: Compare maximal poles
nodes.statement: This is almost immediate if one looks at the maximal poles of both sides. Namely, if $t_k$ is minimal in $\{t_1,\cdots,t_m\}$, the left hand side has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$, and hence the right hand side has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal $t_k$ gives a maximal pole of both sides at $s=-t_k$.

nodes.name: Match a parameter
nodes.statement: But each maximal pole of the right hand side occurs at $s=-t'_l$ for some $t'_l$ which is minimal in $\{t'_1,\dots,t'_{m'}\}$. Hence $t_k=t'_l$ for some $l$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximal poles of the RHS come from minimal $t'_l$, so $t_k=t'_l$.

nodes.name: Cancel matched factors
nodes.statement: After reordering the indices, if necessary, we may assume $t_1=t'_1$. Hence \eqref{E:Lemma} is written as \[ F(s)\cdot\prod_{i=2}^m\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=2}^{m'}\Gamma(s+t'_j). \]
nodes.statement_short: Reorder so $t_1=t'_1$ and cancel one gamma factor from each side.

nodes.name: Induct
nodes.statement: By arguing inductively, one proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by induction on the number of factors.

nodes.name: Proof of the complex case: reduction
nodes.statement: We will prove our main theorem for $F=\mathbb C$. Let $\pi$ and $\pi'$ be infinitesimal equivalence classes of irreducible admissible representations of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$, and assume that their corresponding Langlands parameters $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are given by \begin{align*} \varphi&=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}\\ \varphi'&=\chi_{-N'_1,t'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N'_n, t'_n}. \end{align*} The assertion $L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s, \pi'\times\tau)$ for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_1$ is the same as \begin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M, s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$. As in \eqref{E:twisted_general_parameter_C}, we have \begin{align*} \varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s}&=\chi_{-(N_1+M),t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N_n+M), t_n+s}\\ \varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M,s}& =\chi_{-(N'_1+M),t'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N'_n+M),t'_n+s}, \end{align*} and hence the equality \eqref{E:L-equality-C0} implies \begin{equation} \prod_{i=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N_i+M),t_i+s}) =\prod_{j=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N'_j+M),t'_j+s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$. We will show \eqref{E:L-equality-C} implies $\varphi=\varphi'$. But once we show that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have a common constituent, the theorem follows by induction. Namely, it suffices to prove \begin{equation} \chi_{-N_i, t_i}=\chi_{-N'_j, t'_j} \end{equation} for some $i, j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. The basic idea of our proof is that we will examine ``maximal poles'' of both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C} for different choices of $M$. Our proof has three major steps, which is outlined as follows. In Step 1, we will show that $\{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\}$ as multisets. In Step 2, we will show that $\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}=\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}$. Finally in Step 3, we will finish up the proof of the theorem. In each of the steps we will choose an appropriate $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to Langlands parameters, rewrite $L$-factor equality under all $\chi_{-M,s}$-twists as gamma products; by induction it suffices to find one common constituent.

nodes.name: Set up parameters
nodes.statement: We will prove our main theorem for $F=\mathbb C$. Let $\pi$ and $\pi'$ be infinitesimal equivalence classes of irreducible admissible representations of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$, and assume that their corresponding Langlands parameters $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are given by \begin{align*} \varphi&=\chi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N_n, t_n}\\ \varphi'&=\chi_{-N'_1,t'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-N'_n, t'_n}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write the Langlands parameters of $\pi,\pi'$ as sums of characters.

nodes.name: Restate hypothesis on parameters
nodes.statement: The assertion $L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s, \pi'\times\tau)$ for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_1$ is the same as \begin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M, s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$.
nodes.statement_short: Hypothesis becomes equality of $L$-factors of twisted parameters, (4.1).

nodes.name: Expand twisted L-factors
nodes.statement: As in \eqref{E:twisted_general_parameter_C}, we have \begin{align*} \varphi\otimes\chi_{-M,s}&=\chi_{-(N_1+M),t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N_n+M), t_n+s}\\ \varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M,s}& =\chi_{-(N'_1+M),t'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\chi_{-(N'_n+M),t'_n+s}, \end{align*} and hence the equality \eqref{E:L-equality-C0} implies \begin{equation} \prod_{i=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N_i+M),t_i+s}) =\prod_{j=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N'_j+M),t'_j+s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand twists by (2.12) to get the product identity (4.2).

nodes.name: Reduce to a common constituent
nodes.statement: We will show \eqref{E:L-equality-C} implies $\varphi=\varphi'$. But once we show that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have a common constituent, the theorem follows by induction. Namely, it suffices to prove \begin{equation} \chi_{-N_i, t_i}=\chi_{-N'_j, t'_j} \end{equation} for some $i, j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$.
nodes.statement_short: By induction it suffices to find one common constituent (4.3).

nodes.name: Outline of the three steps
nodes.statement: The basic idea of our proof is that we will examine ``maximal poles'' of both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C} for different choices of $M$. Our proof has three major steps, which is outlined as follows. In Step 1, we will show that $\{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\}$ as multisets. In Step 2, we will show that $\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}=\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}$. Finally in Step 3, we will finish up the proof of the theorem. In each of the steps we will choose an appropriate $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: compare maximal poles for well-chosen $M$ in three steps.

nodes.name: L-equality under GL(1)-twists (complex)
nodes.statement: L(\varphi\otimes\chi_{-M, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\chi_{-M, s})
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C0

nodes.name: product form of L-equality (complex)
nodes.statement: \prod_{i=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N_i+M),t_i+s}) =\prod_{j=1}^nL(\chi_{-(N'_j+M),t'_j+s})
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C

nodes.name: goal: common constituent (complex)
nodes.statement: \chi_{-N_i, t_i}=\chi_{-N'_j, t'_j}
nodes.label: E:goal

nodes.name: Proof of the complex case, Step 1
nodes.statement: Let us choose $M$ large enough so that $N_i+M> 0$ and $N'_j+M>0$ for all $i, j\in\{1,\cdots,n\}$. By \eqref{E:L-factor-C}, we can write \eqref{E:L-equality-C} as \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j) \] for some function $F(s)$ without a pole or zero. Hence by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we have \[ \{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\} \] as multisets.
nodes.statement_short: Twist by large $M$ so all $L$-factors are $\Gamma(s+t_i)$ up to units; Lemma 3.1 gives $\{t_i\}=\{t'_j\}$.

nodes.name: Choose large M and rewrite
nodes.statement: Let us choose $M$ large enough so that $N_i+M> 0$ and $N'_j+M>0$ for all $i, j\in\{1,\cdots,n\}$. By \eqref{E:L-factor-C}, we can write \eqref{E:L-equality-C} as \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j) \] for some function $F(s)$ without a pole or zero.
nodes.statement_short: With $M$ large, (4.2) becomes a gamma-product identity.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: Hence by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we have \[ \{t_1,\dots, t_n\}=\{t'_1,\dots, t'_n\} \] as multisets.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.1 gives equality of the multisets of $t$'s.

nodes.name: Proof of the complex case, Step 2
nodes.statement:
Let us first note that we can now reorder the indices $i$ and $j$ in such a way that  egin{equation} t_1=t'_1, t_2=t'_2,\dots, t_n=t'_n. \end{equation} Let  egin{align*} N_{\min}:=&\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}\ N'_{\min}:=&\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}. \end{align*} As we mentioned above, we will show $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$ in this step. First assume $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$. Choose $M=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is written as  egin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j), \end{equation} where \[ \varepsilon_j= egin{cases}1,\quad	ext{if $N'_j=N'_{\min}$};\ 0,\quad	ext{if $N'_j>N'_{\min}$}, \end{cases} \] and $\varepsilon_j
eq 0$ for at least one $j$. Now the left hand side of \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$ for some $t_k$ which is minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$. Then $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$ and $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ is minimal in $\{t'_1+\varepsilon_1,\dots,t'_n+\varepsilon_n\}$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then we have $t'_l+\varepsilon_l=t_l+1$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, which implies $t_l+1=t_k$. But then $t_l\prec t_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $t_k$. Hence $\varepsilon_l=0$, namely $t_k=t'_l$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} is now written as  egin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i
eq k}\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j
eq l}\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j). \end{equation} by cancelling $\Gamma (s+t_k)$ from the left and $\Gamma (s+t'_l)$ from the right. By arguing inductively, one can show that $\varepsilon_j=0$ for all $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ which is a contradiction. Hence we must have $N'_{\min}\geq N_{\min}$. By symmetry, we can show that $N'_{\min}\leq N_{\min}$. Hence $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$ by contradiction: twist by $M=-N'_{\min}-1$, match maximal poles and cancel inductively.

nodes.name: Reorder indices
nodes.statement: Let us first note that we can now reorder the indices $i$ and $j$ in such a way that \begin{equation} t_1=t'_1, t_2=t'_2,\dots, t_n=t'_n. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reorder so $t_i=t'_i$ (4.4).

nodes.name: Define N_min
nodes.statement: Let \begin{align*} N_{\min}:=&\min\{N_1,\dots,N_n\}\\ N'_{\min}:=&\min\{N'_1,\dots,N'_n\}. \end{align*} As we mentioned above, we will show $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$ in this step.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $N_{\min}$, $N'_{\min}$; goal is their equality.

nodes.name: Assume N'_min < N_min and twist
nodes.statement: First assume $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$. Choose $M=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j), \end{equation} where \[ \varepsilon_j=\begin{cases}1,\quad\text{if $N'_j=N'_{\min}$};\\ 0,\quad\text{if $N'_j>N'_{\min}$}, \end{cases} \] and $\varepsilon_j\neq 0$ for at least one $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$, twist by $M=-N'_{\min}-1$ to get (4.5).

nodes.name: Locate a maximal pole
nodes.statement: Now the left hand side of \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} has a maximal pole at $s=-t_k$ for some $t_k$ which is minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}$. Then $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$ and $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ is minimal in $\{t'_1+\varepsilon_1,\dots,t'_n+\varepsilon_n\}$.
nodes.statement_short: A maximal pole at $-t_k$ forces $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ with minimality.

nodes.name: Rule out epsilon_l = 1
nodes.statement: Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then we have $t'_l+\varepsilon_l=t_l+1$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, which implies $t_l+1=t_k$. But then $t_l\prec t_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $t_k$. Hence $\varepsilon_l=0$, namely $t_k=t'_l$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon_l=1$ contradicts minimality of $t_k$, so $t_k=t'_l$.

nodes.name: Cancel factors
nodes.statement: Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C1} is now written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i\neq k}\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j\neq l}\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j). \end{equation} by cancelling $\Gamma (s+t_k)$ from the left and $\Gamma (s+t'_l)$ from the right.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel the matched gamma factors to get (4.6).

nodes.name: Induct to a contradiction
nodes.statement: By arguing inductively, one can show that $\varepsilon_j=0$ for all $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ which is a contradiction. Hence we must have $N'_{\min}\geq N_{\min}$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductively all $\varepsilon_j=0$, a contradiction; so $N'_{\min}\ge N_{\min}$.

nodes.name: Symmetry
nodes.statement: By symmetry, we can show that $N'_{\min}\leq N_{\min}$. Hence $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$.

nodes.name: twisted gamma identity (Step 2)
nodes.statement: F(s)\prod_{i=1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j),
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C1

nodes.name: after cancellation (Step 2)
nodes.statement: F(s)\prod_{i\neq k}\Gamma(s+t_i)=\prod_{j\neq l}\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j).
nodes.label: E:L-equality-C2

nodes.name: Proof of the complex case, Step 3
nodes.statement: Finally, we will show \eqref{E:goal} for some $i$ and $j$, which will complete the proof of the theorem. For this purpose, let us reorder the indices so that \begin{equation} N_1=N_2=\cdots=N_d<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_n, \end{equation} while still keeping the relation \eqref{E:relation2}. Such indexing is certainly possible. Now let us twist $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ with $M=-N_1-1=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is now written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+t_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i) =\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j) \end{equation} where $\varepsilon_j$ is as before and $\varepsilon_j=1$ for at least one $j$. Let \begin{align*} A&:=A_1\cup A_2, \quad A_1:=\{t_i+1:i\in\{1,\dots,d\}\},\quad A_2:=\{t_i:i\in\{d+1,\dots,n\}\}\\ B&:=\{t'_j+\varepsilon_j: j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\}. \end{align*} Of course by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we know $A=B$ as multisets. We will again look at ``maximal poles'' of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}, which correspond to minimal elements of $A=B$. We consider the following two cases, depending on whether a minimal element is in $A_1$ or $A_2$. First assume $t_k+1\in A_1$ with $k\leq d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we have $t_k+1=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then this means $N'_l=N_1=N_k$ and $t_k=t'_l$. Hence we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=k$ and $j=l$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=0$. First assume $\varepsilon_k=0$. Then $t'_k+\varepsilon_k=t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l-1$, namely $t'_k+\varepsilon_k\prec t'_l+\varepsilon_l$, which contradicts the minimality of $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$. Hence $\varepsilon_k=1$, which implies $N'_k=N_1=N_k$. Since $t_k=t'_k$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, the equality \eqref{E:goal} is satisfied with $i=j=k$. Next assume that $t_k\in A_2$ with $k>d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we know that $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$, so $t_k=t'_l+1=t_l+1$. Then $t_l\prec t_k$. Since $t_k$ is minimal in $A$, we must have $l\leq d$. Hence $N_l=N_1$. Also since $\varepsilon_l=1$ implies $N'_l=N_1$, we have $N'_l=N_l$. Hence, we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=j=l$. Finally assume $\varepsilon_l=0$, \text{i.e.\ } $t_k=t'_l$. Then we can reorder the indices $j$ for the multiset $B$ by swapping $k$ and $l$ without changing the relations \eqref{E:relation2} and \eqref{E:relation1}. So we can cancel $\Gamma(s+t_k)$ from both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}. We can now argue inductively by repeating the above arguments until we obtain \eqref{E:goal}. The proof is complete.

nodes.name: Reorder by N
nodes.statement: Finally, we will show \eqref{E:goal} for some $i$ and $j$, which will complete the proof of the theorem. For this purpose, let us reorder the indices so that \begin{equation} N_1=N_2=\cdots=N_d<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_n, \end{equation} while still keeping the relation \eqref{E:relation2}. nodes.name: Twist by M=-N_1-1
nodes.statement: Now let us twist $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ by $\chi_{-M,s}$ with $M=-N_1-1=-N'_{\min}-1$. Then \eqref{E:L-equality-C} is now written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+t_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^n\Gamma(s+t_i) =\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(s+t'_j+\varepsilon_j) \end{equation} where $\varepsilon_j$ is as before and $\varepsilon_j=1$ for at least one $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting gives identity (4.8).

nodes.name: Multisets A and B
nodes.statement: Let \begin{align*} A&:=A_1\cup A_2, \quad A_1:=\{t_i+1:i\in\{1,\dots,d\}\},\quad A_2:=\{t_i:i\in\{d+1,\dots,n\}\}\\ B&:=\{t'_j+\varepsilon_j: j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\}. \end{align*} Of course by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we know $A=B$ as multisets.
nodes.statement_short: Define $A=A_1\cup A_2$ and $B$; Lemma 3.1 gives $A=B$.

nodes.name: Plan case split
nodes.statement: We will again look at ``maximal poles'' of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}, which correspond to minimal elements of $A=B$. We consider the following two cases, depending on whether a minimal element is in $A_1$ or $A_2$.

nodes.name: Case: minimum in A_1
nodes.statement: First assume $t_k+1\in A_1$ with $k\leq d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we have $t_k+1=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then this means $N'_l=N_1=N_k$ and $t_k=t'_l$. Hence we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=k$ and $j=l$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=0$. First assume $\varepsilon_k=0$. nodes.name: Match in B
nodes.statement: First assume $t_k+1\in A_1$ with $k\leq d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we have $t_k+1=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$.

nodes.name: Subcase epsilon_l=1
nodes.statement: Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$. Then this means $N'_l=N_1=N_k$ and $t_k=t'_l$. Hence we have \eqref{E:goal} with $i=k$ and $j=l$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon_l=1$ gives (4.3) with $i=k$, $j=l$.

nodes.name: Subcase epsilon_l=0
nodes.statement: Assume $\varepsilon_l=0$. First assume $\varepsilon_k=0$. Then $t'_k+\varepsilon_k=t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l-1$, namely $t'_k+\varepsilon_k\prec t'_l+\varepsilon_l$, which contradicts the minimality of $t'_l+\varepsilon_l$. Hence $\varepsilon_k=1$, which implies $N'_k=N_1=N_k$. Since $t_k=t'_k$ by \eqref{E:relation2}, the equality \eqref{E:goal} is satisfied with $i=j=k$.

nodes.name: Case: minimum in A_2
nodes.statement: Next assume that $t_k\in A_2$ with $k>d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we know that $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$. Assume $\varepsilon_l=1$, so $t_k=t'_l+1=t_l+1$. Then $t_l\prec t_k$. Since $t_k$ is minimal in $A$, we must have $l\leq d$. Hence $N_l=N_1$. nodes.name: Match in B
nodes.statement: Next assume that $t_k\in A_2$ with $k>d$ is minmal in $A$. By $A=B$, we know that $t_k=t'_l+\varepsilon_l$ for some $l$, which is minimal in $B$.

nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon_l=1$ forces $l\le d$ and gives (4.3) with $i=j=l$.

nodes.name: Subcase epsilon_l=0
nodes.statement: Finally assume $\varepsilon_l=0$, \text{i.e.\ } $t_k=t'_l$. Then we can reorder the indices $j$ for the multiset $B$ by swapping $k$ and $l$ without changing the relations \eqref{E:relation2} and \eqref{E:relation1}. So we can cancel $\Gamma(s+t_k)$ from both sides of \eqref{E:L-equality-C3}. We can now argue inductively by repeating the above arguments until we obtain \eqref{E:goal}. The proof is complete.

nodes.name: Proof of the real case: setup
nodes.statement: We will prove our main theorem for $F=\mathbb{R}$. Assume $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that $L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s,\pi'\times\tau)$ for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ with $t=1,2$. Namely if $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are the corresponding Langlands parameters, we have \begin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\varepsilon,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\varepsilon,s}) \end{equation} for all $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$, and \begin{equation} L(\varphi\otimes\varphi_{-M,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\varphi_{-M,s}) \end{equation} for all $M\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in\mathbb C$. Let us write \begin{align*} \varphi&=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1,t_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p,t_p}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\right)\\ \varphi'&=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon'_1,t'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_{p'},t'_{p'}}\right)\oplus \left(\varphi_{-N'_1,u'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N'_{q'} u'_{q'}}\right) \end{align*} where we may assume $N_i>0$ and $N'_j>0$ for all $i, j$. Note that the numbers of 1-dimensional constituents for $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are, respectively, $p$ and $p'$, and those for 2-dimensional ones are, respectively, $q$ and $q'$, so $n=p+2q=p'+2q'$.\\ The proof has three steps, and the basic philosophy is the same as the complex case in that we choose appropriate twists and examine ``maximal poles''. In Step 1, we will show $\{u_1, ..., u_q\}=\{u'_1, ..., u'_{q'} \}$ and $\{t_1-\varepsilon_1, ..., t_p-\varepsilon_p\}=\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1, ..., t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}$ as multisets, which also implies $p=p'$ and $q=q'$. In Step 2, we will show the 1-dimensional constituents are equal. Finally in Step 3, we will show the 2-dimensional constituents are equal.
nodes.statement_short: Translate the hypothesis into $L$-factor equalities of parameters under $\lambda$- and $\varphi_{-M,s}$-twists; outline three steps.

nodes.name: Restate hypothesis
nodes.statement: We will prove our main theorem for $F=\mathbb{R}$. Assume $\pi, \pi'\in\operatorname{Irr}_n$ are such that $L(s, \pi\times\tau)=L(s,\pi'\times\tau)$ for all $\tau\in\operatorname{Irr}_t$ with $t=1,2$. Note that the numbers of 1-dimensional constituents for $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are, respectively, $p$ and $p'$, and those for 2-dimensional ones are, respectively, $q$ and $q'$, so $n=p+2q=p'+2q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $\varphi,\varphi'$ into 1- and 2-dimensional constituents.

nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement: The proof has three steps, and the basic philosophy is the same as the complex case in that we choose appropriate twists and examine ``maximal poles''. In Step 1, we will show $\{u_1, ..., u_q\}=\{u'_1, ..., u'_{q'} \}$ and $\{t_1-\varepsilon_1, ..., t_p-\varepsilon_p\}=\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1, ..., t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}$ as multisets, which also implies $p=p'$ and $q=q'$. In Step 2, we will show the 1-dimensional constituents are equal. Finally in Step 3, we will show the 2-dimensional constituents are equal.

otag=&\{t'_j-\varepsilon'_j: j

eq l\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\} \cup\{u'_1-1,\dots,u'_{q'}-1\}. \end{align*} If the latter is the case, namely if $t_k-\varepsilon_k=u'_l$, then by \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}, $u'_l-1=t_k-\varepsilon_k-1$ is a minimal element in both sides of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}. But since $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ is minimal in the left hand side of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0}, $t_k-\varepsilon_k-1$, which is strictly smaller than $t_k-\varepsilon_k$, has to be among $\{u_1-1,\dots,u_q-1\}$. Namely, $t_k-\varepsilon_k-1=u_m-1$ for some $m$, which implies \[ u_m=u'_l. \] Hence by eliminating $u_m$ and $u'_l$, we can shrink both \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1} and obtain  egin{align*} &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_i:i
eq m\}\cup\{u_i:i
eq m\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_j:j
eq l\}\cup\{u'_j:j
eq l\}, \end{align*} and  egin{align*} &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_i:i
eq m\}\cup\{u_i-1:i
eq m\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_j:j
eq l\}\cup\{u'_j-1:j
eq l\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A minimal $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ matches a $t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ or forces $u_m=u'_l$; shrink the multisets.

nodes.name: Two possibilities
nodes.statement: First assume $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ is minimal in the left hand side of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0}. Then either $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_{l'}$ for some $l$, or $t_k-\varepsilon_k=u'_l$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal element matches a 1-dim or a 2-dim entry.

nodes.name: Former case
nodes.statement:
If the former is the case, 	ext{i.e.\ } \[ t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l, \] we can eliminate $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ from the left hand sides of both \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1} and eliminate $t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ from the right hand sides of both \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}, which allows us to shrink the multisets in those two equalities and obtain  egin{align*} &\{t_i-\varepsilon_i: i
eq k\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_j-\varepsilon'_j: j
eq l\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}, \end{align*} and  egin{align*} &\{t_i-\varepsilon_i:i
eq k\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1-1,\dots,u_q-1\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_j-\varepsilon'_j: j
eq l\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\} \cup\{u'_1-1,\dots,u'_{q'}-1\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Eliminate the matched $t$-entries from both identities.

nodes.name: Latter case
nodes.statement:
If the latter is the case, namely if $t_k-\varepsilon_k=u'_l$, then by \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}, $u'_l-1=t_k-\varepsilon_k-1$ is a minimal element in both sides of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}. But since $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ is minimal in the left hand side of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0}, $t_k-\varepsilon_k-1$, which is strictly smaller than $t_k-\varepsilon_k$, has to be among $\{u_1-1,\dots,u_q-1\}$. Namely, $t_k-\varepsilon_k-1=u_m-1$ for some $m$, which implies \[ u_m=u'_l. \] Hence by eliminating $u_m$ and $u'_l$, we can shrink both \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1} and obtain  egin{align*} &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_i:i
eq m\}\cup\{u_i:i
eq m\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_j:j
eq l\}\cup\{u'_j:j
eq l\}, \end{align*} and  egin{align*} &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_i:i
eq m\}\cup\{u_i-1:i
eq m\}\ 
otag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_j:j
eq l\}\cup\{u'_j-1:j
eq l\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Using (5.4), deduce $u_m=u'_l$ and eliminate.

nodes.name: Case: minimum is u_k
nodes.statement: Next assume $u_k$ is a minimal element in the left hand side of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0}. Then either $u_k=u'_l$ or $u_k=t'_l-\varepsilon_l'$ for some $l$. If the former is the case, one can shrink both sides of \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1} as above. If the latter is the case, by arguing in the same way one can obtain $u_k-1=u'_m-1$ for some $m$, which gives $u_k=u'_m$ and allows us to shrink the multisets in \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1} as before.
nodes.statement_short: Same argument when the minimal element is some $u_k$.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: To summarize, at each step one can obtain either $t_i-\varepsilon_i=t'_j-\varepsilon'_j$ or $u_i=u'_j$ for some $i, j$, and by eliminating this element from \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-0} and \eqref{E:multisets_t_u-1}, one can shrink the multisets from those two equalities. But the resulting equalities are of the same form, and hence we can apply the same argument to those two shrunken equalities. By repeating the process, one can obtain \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep} and \eqref{E:multisets_u}, which also imply $p=p'$ and $q=q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat on the shrunken identities to obtain (5.5), (5.6).

nodes.name: multiset identity for M=0
nodes.statement: &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\\ \notag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\},
nodes.label: E:multisets_t_u-0

nodes.name: multiset identity for M=1
nodes.statement: &\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{u_1,\dots,u_q\}\cup\{u_1-1,\dots,u_q-1\}\\ \notag=&\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\cup\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\} \cup\{u'_1-1,\dots,u'_{q'}-1\}
nodes.label: E:multisets_t_u-1

nodes.name: multiset equalities for t-eps and u
nodes.statement: \{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}&=\{t'_1-\varepsilon'_1,\dots,t'_{p'}-\varepsilon'_{p'}\}\\ \{u_1,\dots,u_q\}&=\{u'_1,\dots,u'_{q'}\}
nodes.label: E:multisets_t-ep

nodes.name: Proof of the real case, Step 2
nodes.statement: We will show the 1-dimensional constituents of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are equal. By twisting by $\lambda_{0,s}$, we have \begin{align*} \varphi\otimes\lambda_{0, s} &=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1, t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p, t_p+s}\right) \oplus\left(\varphi_{-N_1, u_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus \varphi_{-N_q, u_q+s}\right)\\ \varphi'\otimes\lambda_{0, s} &=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon'_1, t'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_p, t'_p+s}\right) \oplus\left(\varphi_{-N'_1, u'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus \varphi_{-N'_q, u'_q+s}\right), \end{align*} so the equality $L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{0,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{0,s})$ implies \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_i}{2}\right)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i) =\prod_{j=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t'_j}{2}\right)\cdot\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u'_j), \] where $F(s)$ is a function without a zero or pole. Since we know $\{u_1, ..., u_q\}=\{u'_1, ..., u'_q\}$ as multisets, we have \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_i}{2}\right) =\prod_{j=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t'_j}{2}\right), \] from which we have \begin{equation} \{t_1,\dots,t_p\}=\{t'_1,\dots,t'_p\} \end{equation} as multisets, by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}. By using \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep} and \eqref{E:multisets_t}, we will show that the 1-dimensional constituents of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are equal. But of course, by induction, it suffices to show $\lambda_{\varepsilon_i,t_i}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_j,t'_j}$ for some $i$ and $j$. We will show this by examining minimal elements in those multisets. First, let us note that since we have \eqref{E:multisets_t}, we may reorder the indices so that $t_i=t'_i$ for all $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $t_k=t'_k$ be minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_p\}$. Clearly if $\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon'_k$, then $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k, t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_k, t'_k}$, so we are done. So let us assume $\varepsilon_k\neq\varepsilon'_k$. By symmetry, we may assume $\varepsilon_k=1$ and $\varepsilon'_k=0$. Note, then, that $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ is minimal in $\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}$. By \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep}, we must have $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ for some $l$. Assume $\varepsilon'_l= 0$. Then $t_k-1=t'_l$, which implies $t'_l=t_l\prec t_k$. This contradicts the minimality of $t_k$. Hence $\varepsilon'_l=1=\varepsilon_k$. Then $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ implies $t_l=t'_k$. Namely we have $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k,t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_l, t'_l}$. This completes the proof that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have the same 1-dimensional constituents.
nodes.statement_short: Twist by $\lambda_{0,s}$ to get $\{t_i\}=\{t'_j\}$; combined with (5.5), a minimality argument matches a 1-dimensional constituent, then induct.

nodes.name: Twist by lambda_{0,s}
nodes.statement: We will show the 1-dimensional constituents of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are equal. By twisting by $\lambda_{0,s}$, we have \begin{align*} \varphi\otimes\lambda_{0, s} &=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon_1, t_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_p, t_p+s}\right) \oplus\left(\varphi_{-N_1, u_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus \varphi_{-N_q, u_q+s}\right)\\ \varphi'\otimes\lambda_{0, s} &=\left(\lambda_{\varepsilon'_1, t'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_p, t'_p+s}\right) \oplus\left(\varphi_{-N'_1, u'_1+s}\oplus\cdots\oplus \varphi_{-N'_q, u'_q+s}\right), \end{align*} so the equality $L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{0,s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{0,s})$ implies \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_i}{2}\right)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i) =\prod_{j=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t'_j}{2}\right)\cdot\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u'_j), \] where $F(s)$ is a function without a zero or pole.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting by $\lambda_{0,s}$ gives a gamma identity.

nodes.name: Cancel u's and apply Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: Since we know $\{u_1, ..., u_q\}=\{u'_1, ..., u'_q\}$ as multisets, we have \[ F(s)\prod_{i=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_i}{2}\right) =\prod_{j=1}^{p}\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t'_j}{2}\right), \] from which we have \begin{equation} \{t_1,\dots,t_p\}=\{t'_1,\dots,t'_p\} \end{equation} as multisets, by Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel the $u$-factors by (5.6); Lemma 3.1 gives (5.7).

nodes.name: Reduce to one constituent
nodes.statement: By using \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep} and \eqref{E:multisets_t}, we will show that the 1-dimensional constituents of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are equal. But of course, by induction, it suffices to show $\lambda_{\varepsilon_i,t_i}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_j,t'_j}$ for some $i$ and $j$. We will show this by examining minimal elements in those multisets.
nodes.statement_short: By induction it suffices to match one 1-dimensional constituent.

nodes.name: Minimality argument
nodes.statement: First, let us note that since we have \eqref{E:multisets_t}, we may reorder the indices so that $t_i=t'_i$ for all $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $t_k=t'_k$ be minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_p\}$. Clearly if $\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon'_k$, then $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k, t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_k, t'_k}$, so we are done. So let us assume $\varepsilon_k\neq\varepsilon'_k$. By symmetry, we may assume $\varepsilon_k=1$ and $\varepsilon'_k=0$. Note, then, that $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ is minimal in $\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}$. By \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep}, we must have $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ for some $l$. Assume $\varepsilon'_l= 0$. Then $t_k-1=t'_l$, which implies $t'_l=t_l\prec t_k$. This contradicts the minimality of $t_k$. Hence $\varepsilon'_l=1=\varepsilon_k$. Then $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ implies $t_l=t'_k$. Namely we have $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k,t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_l, t'_l}$. This completes the proof that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have the same 1-dimensional constituents.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal $t_k$ with $\varepsilon_k\ne\varepsilon'_k$ leads to a match $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k,t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_l,t'_l}$.

nodes.name: Choose minimal t_k
nodes.statement: First, let us note that since we have \eqref{E:multisets_t}, we may reorder the indices so that $t_i=t'_i$ for all $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $t_k=t'_k$ be minimal in $\{t_1,\dots,t_p\}$. Clearly if $\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon'_k$, then $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k, t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_k, t'_k}$, so we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Reorder, pick minimal $t_k$; done if $\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon'_k$.

nodes.name: Assume eps_k differs
nodes.statement: So let us assume $\varepsilon_k\neq\varepsilon'_k$. By symmetry, we may assume $\varepsilon_k=1$ and $\varepsilon'_k=0$. Note, then, that $t_k-\varepsilon_k$ is minimal in $\{t_1-\varepsilon_1,\dots,t_p-\varepsilon_p\}$. By \eqref{E:multisets_t-ep}, we must have $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ for some $l$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $\varepsilon_k=1,\varepsilon'_k=0$; (5.5) gives $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$.

nodes.name: Rule out eps'_l=0
nodes.statement: Assume $\varepsilon'_l= 0$. Then $t_k-1=t'_l$, which implies $t'_l=t_l\prec t_k$. This contradicts the minimality of $t_k$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon'_l=0$ contradicts minimality of $t_k$.

nodes.name: Match
nodes.statement: Hence $\varepsilon'_l=1=\varepsilon_k$. Then $t_k-\varepsilon_k=t'_l-\varepsilon'_l$ implies $t_l=t'_k$. Namely we have $\lambda_{\varepsilon_k,t_k}=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_l, t'_l}$. This completes the proof that $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have the same 1-dimensional constituents.
nodes.statement_short: So $\varepsilon'_l=1$ and the constituents match.

nodes.name: Proof of the real case, Step 3
nodes.statement: Finally, we will show that the 2-dimensional constituents are equal. Since we have already shown the 1-dimensional constituents are equal, we may assume \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N'_1,u'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N'_{q'} u'_{q}}. \end{align*} Then the proof is very similar to the complex case. First note that since we already have \eqref{E:multisets_u}, we can reorder the indices in such a way that \begin{equation} u_1=u'_1, u_2=u'_2,\dots, u_n=u'_n. \end{equation} Let us write \begin{align*} N_{\min}&=\min\{N_1,\dots, N'_q\}\\ N'_{\min}&=\min\{N'_1,\dots, N'_q\}, \end{align*} and we will show $N'_{\min}=N_{\min}$. Assume $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$, and consider the twist by $\varphi_{-M, s}$ with $M=N_{\min}$. Then the equality $L(\varphi\otimes\varphi_{-N_{\min},s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\varphi_{-N_{\min},s})$ is written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_{\min})=\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u'_j-M'_j), \quad M'_j=\min\{N'_j, N_{\min}\}, \end{equation} for some $F(s)$ without a zero or a pole, where we used \eqref{E:GL(2)xGL(2)_L}. Let $J=\{j\in\{1,\dots,n\}: N'_j<N_{\min}\}$. By our assumption, $J$ is not empty. Since we have \eqref{E:relation2-R}, the equality \eqref{E:M=M'_j} simplifies to \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i\in J}\Gamma(s+u_i-N_{\min})=\prod_{j\in J}\Gamma(s+u'_j-N'_j). \end{equation} By Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we have \[ \{u_i-N_{\min}: i\in J\}=\{u'_j-N'_j: j\in J\} \] as multisets. Now suppose $u_k-N_{\min}$ is minimal in the left hand side, which is the same as supposing $u_k$ is minimal in $\{u_i: i\in J\}$. There exists $l\in J$ such that $u_k-N_{\min}=u'_l-N'_l$, which gives $u_k=u'_l+(N_{\min}-N'_l)$. Since $N_{\min}-N'_l>0$, this implies $u_l=u'_l\prec u_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $u_k$. Hence $N'_{\min}\geq N_{\min}$. By symmetry, we have $N'_{\min}\leq N_{\min}$, namely $N'_{\min}=N_{\min}$. Then we can proceed analogously to Step 3 of the complex case. Namely, first let us reorder the indices so that in addition to \eqref{E:relation2-R} we have \begin{equation} 0<N_1=\cdots=N_{d}<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_q. \end{equation} By twisting by $\varphi_{-M,s}$ with $M=N_1+1$, we have \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1)\prod_{i=d+1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1-1) =\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1-1+\varepsilon_j), \end{equation} where \[ \varepsilon_j=\begin{cases}1,\quad\text{if $N'_j=N_1=N'_{\min}$}\\ 0,\quad\text{if $N'_j>N_1$}. \end{cases} \] By shifting $s\mapsto s+N_1+1$, the equality \eqref{E:L-equality-R3} becomes \begin{equation} F(s+N_1+1)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+u_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i) =\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i+\varepsilon_j). \end{equation} This is exactly the same as \eqref{E:L-equality-C3} of the complex case. Hence by arguing in the same way, we can show that there exists a pair of indices $i$ and $j$ such that $u_i=u'_j$ and $N_i=N'_j$. Hence for such indices, we have $\varphi_{-N_i, u_i}=\varphi_{-N'_j, u'_j}$, namely $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have a common constituent. By arguing inductively, we have $\varphi=\varphi'$. The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Show $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$ by a minimality contradiction, then twist by $\varphi_{-(N_1+1),s}$ and shift to reduce to the complex-case identity (4.8).

nodes.name: Reduce to 2-dimensional parts
nodes.statement: Finally, we will show that the 2-dimensional constituents are equal. Since we have already shown the 1-dimensional constituents are equal, we may assume \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N_1,u_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N_q, u_q}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N'_1,u'_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\varphi_{-N'_{q'} u'_{q}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Drop the equal 1-dimensional constituents.

nodes.name: Reorder u's
nodes.statement: Then the proof is very similar to the complex case. First note that since we already have \eqref{E:multisets_u}, we can reorder the indices in such a way that \begin{equation} u_1=u'_1, u_2=u'_2,\dots, u_n=u'_n. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reorder so $u_i=u'_i$ (5.8).

nodes.name: Define N_min
nodes.statement: Let us write \begin{align*} N_{\min}&=\min\{N_1,\dots, N'_q\}\\ N'_{\min}&=\min\{N'_1,\dots, N'_q\}, \end{align*} and we will show $N'_{\min}=N_{\min}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $N_{\min}$, $N'_{\min}$.

nodes.name: Assume N'_min<N_min and twist
nodes.statement: Assume $N'_{\min}<N_{\min}$, and consider the twist by $\varphi_{-M, s}$ with $M=N_{\min}$. Then the equality $L(\varphi\otimes\varphi_{-N_{\min},s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\varphi_{-N_{\min},s})$ is written as \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_{\min})=\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u'_j-M'_j), \quad M'_j=\min\{N'_j, N_{\min}\}, \end{equation} for some $F(s)$ without a zero or a pole, where we used \eqref{E:GL(2)xGL(2)_L}.
nodes.statement_short: Twist by $\varphi_{-N_{\min},s}$ to obtain (5.9).

nodes.name: Restrict to J
nodes.statement: Let $J=\{j\in\{1,\dots,n\}: N'_j<N_{\min}\}$. By our assumption, $J$ is not empty. Since we have \eqref{E:relation2-R}, the equality \eqref{E:M=M'_j} simplifies to \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i\in J}\Gamma(s+u_i-N_{\min})=\prod_{j\in J}\Gamma(s+u'_j-N'_j). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Cancel factors outside $J$ to get (5.10).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we have \[ \{u_i-N_{\min}: i\in J\}=\{u'_j-N'_j: j\in J\} \] as multisets.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.1 equates the shifted multisets over $J$.

nodes.name: Minimality contradiction
nodes.statement: Now suppose $u_k-N_{\min}$ is minimal in the left hand side, which is the same as supposing $u_k$ is minimal in $\{u_i: i\in J\}$. There exists $l\in J$ such that $u_k-N_{\min}=u'_l-N'_l$, which gives $u_k=u'_l+(N_{\min}-N'_l)$. Since $N_{\min}-N'_l>0$, this implies $u_l=u'_l\prec u_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $u_k$. Hence $N'_{\min}\geq N_{\min}$. By symmetry, we have $N'_{\min}\leq N_{\min}$, namely $N'_{\min}=N_{\min}$.
nodes.statement_short: A minimal $u_k$ leads to $u_l\prec u_k$, contradiction; hence $N_{\min}=N'_{\min}$.

nodes.name: Reorder N's
nodes.statement: Then we can proceed analogously to Step 3 of the complex case. Namely, first let us reorder the indices so that in addition to \eqref{E:relation2-R} we have \begin{equation} 0<N_1=\cdots=N_{d}<N_{d+1}\leq\cdots\leq N_q. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reorder so $N_1=\dots=N_d<N_{d+1}\le\cdots$ (5.11).

nodes.name: Twist by phi_{-(N_1+1),s}
nodes.statement: By twisting by $\varphi_{-M,s}$ with $M=N_1+1$, we have \begin{equation} F(s)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1)\prod_{i=d+1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1-1) =\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i-N_1-1+\varepsilon_j), \end{equation} where \[ \varepsilon_j=\begin{cases}1,\quad\text{if $N'_j=N_1=N'_{\min}$}\\ 0,\quad\text{if $N'_j>N_1$}. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Twisting gives (5.12).

nodes.name: Shift to complex-case identity
nodes.statement: By shifting $s\mapsto s+N_1+1$, the equality \eqref{E:L-equality-R3} becomes \begin{equation} F(s+N_1+1)\prod_{i=1}^d\Gamma(s+u_i+1)\cdot\prod_{i=d+1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i) =\prod_{j=1}^q\Gamma(s+u_i+\varepsilon_j). \end{equation} This is exactly the same as \eqref{E:L-equality-C3} of the complex case.
nodes.statement_short: Shift $s$ to obtain (5.13), identical to (4.8).

nodes.name: Conclude as in complex case
nodes.statement: Hence by arguing in the same way, we can show that there exists a pair of indices $i$ and $j$ such that $u_i=u'_j$ and $N_i=N'_j$. Hence for such indices, we have $\varphi_{-N_i, u_i}=\varphi_{-N'_j, u'_j}$, namely $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ have a common constituent. By arguing inductively, we have $\varphi=\varphi'$. The proof is complete.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.2
nodes.statement: We will give a proof only for $n=3$. (The cae for $n=2$ is simpler and left to the reader.) Assume $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ are the local Langlands parameters for $\pi$ and $\pi'$. First assume \begin{align} \varphi&=\lambda_{\varepsilon_1, t_1}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_2, t_2}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_3, t_3}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N', u'}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon', t'} \end{align} with $N'>0$, and we will derive a contradiction. First note that the assumption on the central characters implies \begin{equation} -(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2+\varepsilon_3)+t_1+t_2+t_3=2u'-N'-\varepsilon'+t', \end{equation} where we used \eqref{E:central_character} to obtain the right hand side. Next note that for each $\lambda_{\delta, s}$ we have \begin{align*} \varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s} &=\lambda_{\delta_1, t_1+s-\gamma_1}\oplus\lambda_{\delta_2, t_2+s-\gamma_2}\oplus \lambda_{\delta_3, t_3+s-\gamma_3}\\ \varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s} &=\varphi_{-N',u'+s-\delta}\oplus\lambda_{\delta', t'+s-\gamma'} \end{align*} where $\delta_i=\varepsilon_i+\delta\pmod{2}$ and $\gamma_i=2$ (resp.\ 0) if $\varepsilon_i=\delta=1$ (resp.\ otherwise), and similarly for $\delta'$ and $\gamma'$. Now the equality of the $L$-functions implies \[ F(s)\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_1-\gamma_1}{2}\right)\cdot \Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_2-\gamma_2}{2}\right)\cdot \Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_3-\gamma_3}{2}\right) =\Gamma(s+u'-\delta)\cdot \Gamma\left(\frac{s+t'-\gamma'}{2}\right) \] for some $F(s)$ without a zero or pole, which is, by the duplication formula, written as \begin{align*} F(s)&\Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_1-\gamma_1}{2}\right)\cdot \Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_2-\gamma_2}{2}\right)\cdot \Gamma\left(\frac{s+t_3-\gamma_3}{2}\right)\\ =&\Gamma\left(\frac{s+u'-\delta}{2}\right)\cdot \Gamma\left(\frac{s+u'-\delta+1}{2}\right)\cdot \Gamma\left(\frac{s+t'-\gamma'}{2}\right) \end{align*} for some other $F(s)$. By Lemma \ref{L:Lemma}, we have \begin{equation} \{t_1-\gamma_1, t_2-\gamma_2, t_3-\gamma_3\} =\{u'-\delta, u'-\delta+1, t'-\gamma'\} \end{equation} as multisets. First choose $\delta=0$, which forces $\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\gamma_3=\gamma'=0$, and hence we have \[ \{t_1, t_2, t_3\}=\{u', u'+1, t'\} \] as multisets. Up to reordering of the indices, we may assume \[ t_1=u', t_2=u'+1, t_3=t', \] which makes \eqref{E:multisets_GL(3)} into \begin{equation} \{t_1-\gamma_1, t_1+1-\gamma_2, t_3-\gamma_3\} =\{t_1-\delta, t_1+1-\delta, t_3-\gamma'\}. \end{equation} Also note that the central character assumption \eqref{E:central} implies \[ -(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2+\varepsilon_3)+u'+u'+1+t'=2u'-N'-\varepsilon'+t', \] which gives \[ N'=(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2+\varepsilon_3)-\varepsilon'-1. \] Since $N'>0$, we must always have \begin{equation} \varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2+\varepsilon_3-\varepsilon'>1. \end{equation} By letting $\delta=1$ in \eqref{E:multisets_GL(3)-1}, we have \begin{equation} \{t_1-\gamma_1, t_1+1-\gamma_2, t_3-\gamma_3\} =\{t_1-1, t_1, t_3-\gamma'\}. \end{equation} Assume $t_1-\gamma_1$ is a minimal element in the left hand side . Then we must have $\gamma_1=2$ (so $\varepsilon_1=1$), because $t_1-1$ is in the left hand side and so we must have $t_1-\gamma_1\preceq t_1-1$, and hence we have \[ \{t_1-2, t_1+1-\gamma_2, t_3-\gamma_3\} =\{t_1-1, t_1, t_3-\gamma'\}. \] Then we must have $t_1-2=t_3-\gamma'$, which implies \[ \{t_1+1-\gamma_2, t_1-2-\gamma_3+\gamma'\} =\{t_1-1, t_1\}. \] Considering $1-\gamma_2$ is always odd, we conclude $t_1+1-\gamma_2=t_1-1$, which implies $\gamma_2=2$ (so $\varepsilon_2=1$), and $t_1-2-\gamma_3+\gamma'=t_1$, which implies $\gamma_3=0$ (so $\varepsilon_3=0$) and $\gamma'=2$ (so $\varepsilon'=1$). But this contradicts the condition \eqref{E:epsilon} coming from the central character assumption. Hence $t_1-\gamma_1$ cannot be minimal in the left hand side of \eqref{E:multisets_GL(3)-2}. Suppose now that $t_1+1-\gamma_2$ is minimal. Then this implies that $\gamma_1=0$ and $\gamma_2=2$, in which case $\varepsilon_1=0$ and $\varepsilon_2=1$. Then \eqref{E:multisets_GL(3)-2} implies $t_3-\gamma_3=t_3-\gamma'$, which implies $\gamma_3=\gamma'$, which in turn implies $\varepsilon_3=\varepsilon'$. Then the left hand side of \eqref{E:epsilon} will be $1$, which is a contradiction. Hence neither $t_1-\gamma_1$ nor $t_2+1-\gamma_2$ can be minimal. So $t_3-\gamma_3$ can be the only minimal element, which means \[ t_3-\gamma_3\prec t_1-1\prec t_1 \] or \[ t_3-\gamma_3\prec t_1-2\prec t_1+1-\gamma_2. \] The first case comes from the situation where $\gamma_1 = 0, \gamma_2 = 2$, which we argued earlier cannot happen. We consider the second case. Notice that all the elements are comparable and the inequalities are all strict. Hence the same has to happen in the right hand side. But one can easily see that this is impossible because the right hand side already contains $t_1-1$ and $t_1$ while the second largest element in the left hand side is $t_1-2$. Hence we conclude that we cannot have both \eqref{E:1+1+1} and \eqref{E:2+1} at the same time; namely, if $\varphi$ is a sum of three irreducible representations, so is $\varphi'$, and if $\varphi$ is a sum of two irreducible representations, so is $\varphi'$. First, assume \begin{align*} \varphi&=\lambda_{\varepsilon_1, t_1}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_2, t_2}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon_3, t_3}\\ \varphi'&=\lambda_{\varepsilon'_1, t'_1}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_2, t'_2}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon'_3, t'_3}. \end{align*} Then the argument is similar to Step 2 of the real case. Namely by twisting by $\lambda_{0, s}$ and equating the $L$-factors, one can get \[ \{t_1,t_2,t_3\}=\{t'_1,t'_2,t'_3\} \] as multisets. Also by twisting by $\lambda_{1,s}$ and equating the $L$-factors, one can get \[ \{t_1-\gamma_1,t_2-\gamma_2,t_3-\gamma_3\}= \{t'_1-\gamma'_1,t'_2-\gamma'_2,t'_3-\gamma'_3\} \] as multisets, where $\gamma_i=2$ if $\varepsilon_i=1$, and $\gamma_i=0$ if $\varepsilon_i=0$, and similarly for $\gamma'_i$. Then the argument of Step 2 of the real case goes through with the $\varepsilon$'s replaced by $\gamma$'s. Hence we get $\varphi=\varphi'$. Next, assume \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N, t}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon, u}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N', t'}\oplus\lambda_{\varepsilon', u'}. \end{align*} By twisting $\lambda_{\delta, s}$, equating the $L$-factors and using the duplication formula, one obtains \[ \{t-\delta, t+1-\delta, u-\gamma\}= \{t'-\delta, t'+1-\delta, u'-\gamma'\} \] where $\gamma=2$ if $\varepsilon=\delta=1$ and 0 otherwise, and similarly for $\gamma'$. By examining minimal elements, one can see that this implies $t=t'$, $u=u'$ and $\gamma=\gamma'$ (so $\varepsilon=\varepsilon'$). (The detail is left to the reader.) Finally the central character assumption implies $N=N'$. The proposition follows.

nodes.name: Non-isomorphic GL_2(R) parameters with equal GL(1)-twisted L-factors
nodes.statement: Let \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N, t}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N', t} \end{align*} with $N>0, N'>0$ but $N\neq N'$. Then for any $\lambda_{\delta, s}$, we have \[ L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s})=L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}) =2(2\pi)^{-(t+s-\delta)}\Gamma(t+s-\delta). \] Of course, there are infinitely many such choices for $N$ and $N'$. If we further assume $N=N'\pmod{4}$, not only the $L$-factors but the $\epsilon$-factors coincide. Indeed, we can compute \[ \epsilon(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}, \psi_\mathbb{R})=\epsilon(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta, s}, \psi_\mathbb{R}) =-i^{N+1}=-i^{N'+1}, \] and again there are infinitely many such choices.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_{-N,t}$ and $\varphi_{-N',t}$ with $N\ne N'$ have equal $L$-factors (and, if $N\equiv N'$ mod 4, equal $\epsilon$-factors) under all $\operatorname{GL}(1)$-twists.

nodes.name: GL_4(R) parameters indistinguishable by GL(1)-twists
nodes.statement: Let \begin{align*} \varphi&=\varphi_{-N_1, t_1}\oplus\varphi_{-N_2, t_2}\\ \varphi'&=\varphi_{-N'_1, t'_1}\oplus\varphi_{-N'_2, t'_2}. \end{align*} Let $\omega$ and $\omega'$ be the central characters of the representations corresponding to $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$, respectively. Then by \eqref{E:central_character} we know \begin{align*} \omega(r)&=r^{-(N_1+N_2)+2(t_1+t_2)}\\ \omega'(r)&=r^{-(N'_1+N'_2)+2(t'_1+t'_2)} \end{align*} for $r\in\mathbb{R}^\times$. For each $\lambda_{\delta, s}$, we have \begin{align*} L(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s})&=4(2\pi)^{-(2s+t_1+t_2-2\delta)} \Gamma(s+t_1-\delta)\Gamma(s+t_2-\delta)\\ L(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s})&=4(2\pi)^{-(2s+t'_1+t'_2-2\delta)} \Gamma(s+t'_1-\delta)\Gamma(s+t'_2-\delta) \end{align*} and \begin{align*} \epsilon(\varphi\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}, \psi_\mathbb{R})&=i^{N_1+N_2+2}\\ \epsilon(\varphi'\otimes\lambda_{\delta,s}, \psi_\mathbb{R})&=i^{N'_1+N'_2+2}. \end{align*} Hence if we have \[ N_1+N_2=N'_1+N'_2\quad\text{and}\quad \{t_1, t_2\}=\{t'_1, t'_2\}, \] then the $L$-factors, $\epsilon$-factors and central characters will all coincide. Of course there are infinitely many such choices.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_{-N_1,t_1}\oplus\varphi_{-N_2,t_2}$ vs. $\varphi_{-N'_1,t'_1}\oplus\varphi_{-N'_2,t'_2}$ with $N_1+N_2=N'_1+N'_2$ and equal $\{t_1,t_2\}$ share $L$-, $\epsilon$-factors and central characters.
